home.intro: Backend developer based in Belo Horizonte, finishing my Information Systems degree at UFMG. My days are split between C#/.NET and Java/Spring Boot, and I usually take part in the whole ecosystem: from designing the solution and modeling the data through implementation, testing and final delivery. I like to understand the problem properly before writing code, and to ship services that can grow without drama.

projects.title: Projects
projects.subtitle: Things I built on my own plus university assignments. Filter by technology.
projects.picodohorizonte.description: Backend application for a craft beverages portfolio, enabling administrative management of products, categories, and related content. Designed to support an admin dashboard with secure control over catalog data and business rules.
projects.wifi-bh.description: Web application for managing public Wi-Fi points in Belo Horizonte. Users can add new points, rate existing ones with stars, import data from PBH CSV files, and view all registered points with coordinates and ratings.
projects.bustracker.description: Real-time bus tracking system for Belo Horizonte, using public API data from PBH (Prefeitura de Belo Horizonte). It includes a REST API for querying stops, lines and arrival predictions, a background worker for collecting real-time bus positions, and a GTFS data importer.
projects.investimentos.description: A RESTful API for managing financial investments. Allows registering investments, calculating estimated returns, and viewing dashboards with summaries and charts.
projects.our-places.description: A Java backend API built with Spring for relationship management. Designed for couples, it allows saving and rating visited places, storing important dates, and managing shared memories.
projects.race-manager-api.description: A Java backend API built with Spring for race management. Designed for organizers, it allows creating championships and categories, adding participants, recording finish times, and accessing results.
projects.user-service.description: A backend application for user registration built with a microservices architecture. It includes a User Service to handle new user creation and an Email Service to send a welcome notification upon successful registration.
projects.huffman.description: The project is a program designed to reduce the size of text files using the Huffman compression algorithm. It builds a Huffman tree based on character frequency, encoding frequent characters with shorter binary codes. The program supports both compression and decompression of text files.
projects.convex-hull.description: This C++ project processes 2D point data to compute the convex hull of a point set using Graham's or Jarvis's algorithms. Points are read from a text file, and for Graham's method, the user can choose between InsertionSort, MergeSort, or BucketSort.
projects.p2p-chat.description: This project implements a distributed P2P chat system using a blockchain-inspired consensus mechanism to ensure message history integrity and ordering across network nodes. The entire application was developed in Python, leveraging the asyncio library for asynchronous handling of concurrent network connections.
projects.math-expressions.description: The project is a C++ implementation of a mathematical expression calculator. It includes features for validating and solving complex expressions in both infix and postfix notation. The program can handle parentheses, multiple operators and operands, and expressions up to 1000 characters. It verifies expression validity, converts between notations, and solves them using a simple interface.
projects.rip-over-udp.description: The project is a dynamic routing system based on the RIP protocol over UDP, developed in Python to simulate real routing behavior between multiple routers.
experience.title: Experience
experience.subtitle: Where I've been, what I did and what I worked with at each step.
experience.dev.body: I work across the full development cycle: understanding the need with whoever asked for it, designing the solution, modeling the data, implementing, testing and watching how it behaves once it's live. My time is split between .NET products and Java applications with Spring Boot, and a good part of the job is making different systems talk to each other well without turning into a tangle nobody can maintain.
experience.dev.b1: Development in C# with .NET and .NET Framework: new features, evolving existing modules and refactoring legacy code in small, safe steps.
experience.dev.b2: Java applications with Spring Boot and MySQL — maintenance, new routines, fixing production behavior and performance tuning.
experience.dev.b3: Building and consuming REST APIs between internal and external services, taking care of the data contract and error handling on both ends.
experience.dev.b4: Data modeling and SQL across PostgreSQL, SQL Server and MySQL: writing and tuning queries, indexes, migrations and reading execution plans when something gets slow.
experience.dev.b5: Daily routine on Git and GitLab — branches, merge requests and code review — with services packaged in Docker so they run the same anywhere.
experience.intern.body: My first contact with a genuinely large system: years of history and a lot of people depending on it every day. I spent the internship learning how to find my way around that kind of codebase — understand the flow before touching it, reproduce the problem before proposing a fix, and measure the impact before changing anything.
experience.intern.b1: Analyzing and fixing bugs in C#/.NET applications, digging end to end: from the screen down to the query.
experience.intern.b2: SQL Server every day, used both for diagnosis and for correcting and extracting data.
experience.intern.b3: Delivering new features and usability improvements in existing modules without breaking what already worked.
experience.intern.b4: Maintaining and evolving integrations between modules and services, keeping the communication between them consistent.
experience.pijunior.body: A junior enterprise with real clients and real deadlines. That's where I realized half the work happens before the code: asking a lot of questions, understanding the process of the person who'll use it, and cutting scope that solves nobody's problem. It's also where I wrote plenty of Python.
experience.pijunior.b1: Web applications in Python: interactive dashboards, user authentication and integrations with external REST APIs.
experience.pijunior.b2: Automation of manual, repetitive routines, cutting down time spent and room for human error.
experience.pijunior.b3: Requirements gathering, scope definition and prioritization straight with the client.
experience.ufmg.body: University is where I picked up the foundation I now use without noticing: algorithms and data structures, networking, operating systems and databases. Most assignments were in C++ and Python, solving problems by hand with no framework to lean on — which teaches you fast what each implementation choice actually costs.
about.title: About me
about.p1: I live in Belo Horizonte, Brazil. I've always been into sports — I competed in mountain biking and motocross, and that's where I learned first-hand what discipline, repeated practice and getting back up after a fall really mean. That came along with me into work: a stubborn bug and a long climb have more in common than you'd think.
about.p2: I've been fascinated by computers since I was a kid. What hooked me wasn't the machine itself, it was the feeling of cracking a problem that looked impossible at two in the afternoon and is running by five. That's pretty much why I still do this every day.
about.p3: I'm currently finishing my Information Systems degree at the Federal University of Minas Gerais (UFMG). The course gave me solid ground in algorithms, data structures, networking and databases — subjects that sound theoretical right up until a slow query or a bad data model makes you remember all of them at once.
about.p4: My professional path started at Pi Júnior, where I spent about a year as a Project Analyst. I built web applications in Python — interactive dashboards, user authentication and integrations with external REST APIs — and wrote automations that took a good chunk of repetitive manual work off people's hands. I also gathered requirements with clients, defined scope and prioritized demands, which is where I really learned that understanding the problem is worth more than the most elegant solution.
about.p5: I then joined Group Software as a Software Development Intern, focused on backend. I spent a lot of time inside C#/.NET code I hadn't written, tracking bugs end to end: from the screen down to the query. That was when I learned to read a large system without getting lost, to use SQL Server as a diagnostic tool and not just a place to select from, and to ship new features without breaking what was already there.
about.p6: Today I'm a Software Engineer at the same company, working on .NET products and Java applications with Spring Boot. I won't repeat everything I do day to day here: it's laid out step by step, with the technologies behind each phase, on the experience page.
about.p7: Outside of work I keep studying: I read about architecture, microservices and messaging with RabbitMQ, and I keep personal projects on GitHub precisely so I can try new ideas at no risk. That's where I get to be wrong for free and show up at work already knowing what works.
